name: Wardley Mapping
use_case: A map that positions every component a user need depends on along two axes: how visible it is to the user, and how far it has evolved from novel and custom-built toward standardised commodity. Best used when deciding what to build versus buy versus outsource, when the same capability is being reinvented in several teams, or when a roadmap keeps investing engineering effort into components that the market has already turned into utilities.
strengths: the evolution axis shows what to stop building because the market commoditised it
anchoring on user need prevents maps that flatter internal org structure
makes build-buy-outsource arguments visual instead of rhetorical
exposes where two teams are independently reinventing the same component
weaknesses: placing components on the evolution axis is subjective and hotly argued
steep learning curve; a first map is usually wrong and needs iterating
few practitioners, so facilitation is hard to source
goes stale as components evolve, so it needs periodic redrawing
use_cases: Several government departments each pay for and run their own version of the same IT system, and the central digital team wants to show which of these should become one shared service or be bought as a standard product.
The CIO of a public body wants technology strategy conversations to start from why each system exists and how mature it is in the market, instead of from the usual box-and-line architecture diagrams.

A buyer is drafting a single fixed-price outsourcing contract for an entire system and suspects some of its components are too novel for a supplier to price, which would lead to costly change requests later.

Architects disagree whether a new platform should be developed in-house iteratively or specified in detail and outsourced, although some of its components are novel and others are standard commodities.
